source_text: Quicquid ergo mediocritas nostra ad poenitentiam semel capessendam et perpetuo continendam suggerere conata est, omnes quidem deditos Domino spectat, ut omnis salutis in promerendo Deo petitores, sed praecipue novitiolis istis imminet. Qui cum maxime incipiunt divinis sermonibus aures rigare, quique catuli infantiae adhuc recentis, nec perfectis luminibus incerta reptant; et dicunt quidem pristinis renuntiare, et poenitentiam assumunt, sed includere eam negligunt. Interpellat enim illos ad desiderandum ex pristinis aliquid, ipse finis desiderandi: velut poma cum jam in acorem vel amaritudinem senescere incipiunt, ex parte aliqua tamen adhuc ipsi gratiae suae adulantur. Omne praeterea cunctationis et tergiversationis erga poenitentiam vitium, praesumptio intinctionis importat. Certi enim indubitatae veniae delictorum, medium tempus interim furantur, et commeatum sibi faciunt delinquendi, quam eruditionem non delinquendi. Quam porro ineptum, quam iniquum, poenitentiam non adimplere, et veniam delictorum sustinere, hoc est, pretium non exhibere, ad mercem manum emittere! Hoc enim pretio Dominus veniam addicere instituit; hac poenitentiae compensatione redimendam proponit impunitatem. Si ergo qui venditant, prius nummum, quo paciscuntur, examinant, ne scalptus, neve rasus, ne adulter etiam: Dominum credimus poenitentiae probationem prius inire, tantam nobis mercedem perennis scilicet vitae concessurum? Sed differamus tantisper poenitentiae veritatem. Tunc opinor emendatos liquebit, cum absolvimur? Nullo pacto. Sed cum pendente venia, poena prospicitur, cum adhuc liberari non meremur ut possimus mereri cum Deus comminatur, non cum ignoscit. Quis enim servus, postquam libertate mutatus est, furta sua et fugas sibi imputat? Quis miles postquam castris suis emissus, pro notis suis satagit? Peccator ante veniam deflere se debet; quia tempus poenitentiae, id est, quod periculi et timoris. Neque ego renuo divinum beneficium, id est, abolitionem delictorum inituris aquam omnimodo salvum esse; sed ut eo pervenire contingat, elaborandum est. Quis enim tibi tam infidae poenitentiae viro asperginem unam cujuslibet aquae commodabit? furto quidem aggredi, et praepositum hujus rei asseverationibus tuis circumduci facile est. Sed Deus thesauro suo providet, nec sinit obrepere indignos. Quid denique ait? Nihil occultum, quod non revelabitur. Quantascumque tenebras factis tuis superstruxeris, Deus lumen est. Quidam autem sic opinantur, quasi Deus necesse habeat praestare etiam indignis quod spopondit: et liberalitatem ejus faciunt servitutem. Quod si necessitate nobis, symbolum mortis indulget ergo invitus facit: quis enim permittit permansurum id, quod tribuerit invitus? Non enim multi postea excidunt? non a multis donum illud aufertur? Hi sunt scilicet, qui obrepunt, qui poenitentiae fidem aggressi, super arenas domum ruituram collocant. Nemo ergo sibi aduletur, quia inter auditorum tirocinia deputatur, quasi eo etiam nunc sibi delinquere liceat Dominum simul cognoveris, timeas: simul inspexeris, reverearis. Caeterum quid te cognovisse interest, cum iisdem incubas, quibus retro ignarus? Quid autem te a perfecto servo Dei separat? An alius est intinctis Christus, alius audientibus? Num spes alia, vel merces, alia formido judicii, alia necessitas poenitentiae? Lavacrum illud obsignatio est fidei: quae fides a poenitentiae fide incipitur et commendatur. Non ideo abluimur, ut delinquere desinamus, quoniam jam corde loti sumus. Haec enim prima audientis intinctio est metus integer; exinde quoad Dominum senseris, fides sana, conscientia semel poenitentiam amplexata. Caeterum, si ab aquis peccare desistimus, necessitate, non sponte innocentiam induimus. Quis ergo in bonitate praecellens? cui non licet, aut cui displicet malo esse? qui jubetur, an qui delectatur a crimine vacare? Ergo nec a furto manus avertamus, nisi claustrorum duritia repugnet: nec oculos a stupri concupiscentiis refraenemus, nisi a custodibus corporum obstructi, si nemo Domino deditus delinquere desinet, nisi intinctione alligatus. Quod si qui ita senserit, nescio an intinctus magis contristetur, quod peccare desierit, quam laetetur, quod evaserit. Itaque audientes optare intinctionem, non praesumere oportet. Qui enim optat, honorat: qui praesumit, superbit. In illo verecundia, in isto petulantia apparet. Ille satagit, hic negligit. Ille mereri cupit, at hic, ut debitum, sibi repromittit: ille sumit, hic invadit. Quem censeas digniorem, nisi emendatiorem? quem emendatiorem, nisi timidiorem, et idcirco vera poenitentia functum? Timuit enim adhuc delinquere, ne non mereretur accipere. At ille praesumptor, cum sibi repromitteret, securus scilicet, timere non potuit: sic nec poenitentiam implevit, quia instrumento poenitentiae, id est, metu, caruit. Praesumptio inverecundiae portio est, instat petitorem, despicit datorem. Itaque decipit nonnunquam. Ante enim quam debeatur repromittit, quo semper is, qui est praestaturus, offenditur.
pass_a_gloss: Whatever our mediocrity has attempted to suggest for undertaking repentance once and holding onto it perpetually, it looks to all who are devoted to the Lord, so that all may be petitioners for salvation by meriting it from God, but it especially threatens those new converts who are just beginning to be nourished by divine sermons and are still young and uncertain. Although they do renounce their past and take up repentance, they neglect to enclose themselves in it. For the end of desiring something from their past interrupts them. Just like fruit that has begun to wither or turn bitter, they still partly cling to their old gratifications. Moreover, every fault of hesitation and tergiversation regarding repentance involves the presumption of baptism. For those who are certain of the unquestionable forgiveness of sins, steal away the meantime and make for themselves a pass to sin, which is not the instruction to not sin. How foolish and unjust it is to not fulfill repentance and to sustain the forgiveness of sins, that is, to not exhibit the price, to extend the hand for the merchandise. For the Lord has established this price to grant forgiveness; with this compensation of repentance, He proposes to redeem impunity. If, therefore, those who sell examine the coin beforehand, lest it be counterfeit, clipped, or adulterated, do we believe the Lord enters into the testing of repentance beforehand, to concede to us such a great reward of eternal life? But let us defer the truth of repentance for a while. Then, I think, it will be clear to those who have been corrected, when we are absolved? Not at all. But when punishment is still in prospect, with forgiveness pending, we do not yet merit to be liberated so that we may be able to merit it when God threatens, not when He forgives. For who is the servant, after having been changed to freedom, who imputes his own thefts and flights to himself? Who is the soldier, after having been discharged from the barracks, who strives for his known faults? The sinner ought to lament before receiving forgiveness, because the time for repentance is a time of danger and fear. Nor do I deny the divine benefit, that is, the abolition of sins, to be entirely safe for those who are initiated into the water; but to attain this, one must strive. For who will provide a single aspersion of any water to a man of such unfaithful repentance? It is easy to attack by stealth and to be led around by one's own assertions. But God takes care of His own treasure and does not allow the unworthy to sneak in. What, finally, does He say? Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed. However great the darkness you have built over your deeds, God is light. Some, however, think that God necessarily has to provide what He has promised, even to the unworthy, and they make His liberality a servitude. But if He grants indulgence to us out of necessity, then He does it unwillingly; for who permits what He has given unwillingly to remain? Do not many afterwards fall away? Is not that gift taken away from many? These are the ones who sneak in, who, having attacked the faith of repentance, build a house that will collapse on the sand. Let no one, therefore, deceive himself, because he is reckoned among the beginners, as if it is still permitted for him to sin, now that he has come to know the Lord; let him fear and reverence at the same time. But what does it profit you to have come to know, when you lie in the same things you were ignorant of before? What separates you from a perfect servant of God? Is Christ one thing to the baptized and another to the listeners? Is there another hope, or another reward, or another fear of judgment, or another necessity of repentance? That washing is a seal of faith, which faith begins with and is commended by the faith of repentance. We are not washed so that we may cease to sin, because we have already been washed in heart. For this is the first washing of the listener, a whole fear; from then on, as long as you perceive the Lord, you have healthy faith, a conscience that has once embraced repentance. But if we cease to sin after the waters, it is out of necessity, not spontaneity, that we put on innocence. Who, then, excels in goodness? To whom is it not permitted, or to whom is it displeasing to be evil? Who is commanded, or who delights in being free from crime? Therefore, we do not turn our hands away from theft, unless the harshness of prison opposes us; nor do we restrain our eyes from the desires of lust, unless we are obstructed by the guardians of our bodies. If no one who is devoted to the Lord ceases to sin, unless bound by baptism, what if someone thinks this way? I do not know whether the baptized person is more grieved that he has ceased to sin than he is joyful that he has escaped. Therefore, the listeners ought to wish for baptism, not presume it. For he who wishes, honors; he who presumes, is proud. In the one, there appears modesty; in the other, petulance. The one strives; the other is negligent. The one desires to merit; the other promises it to himself as a debt: the one takes; the other invades. Whom do you consider more worthy, if not the one who is more corrected? Whom more corrected, if not the one who is more fearful, and therefore has performed true repentance? For he has feared to sin anymore, lest he not merit receiving. But the presumptuous one, when he promised it to himself, could not fear, being secure; thus, he did not fulfill repentance, because he lacked the instrument of repentance, that is, fear. Presumption is a part of shamelessness; it presses the petitioner and despises the giver. And so, it sometimes deceives. For before what is due is paid, it promises, by which the one who is to provide is always offended.

pass_b_english: My modest effort to set out the case for repentance—undertaken once, maintained forever—addresses everyone devoted to the Lord, all of them petitioners for salvation earned from God; yet it bears down hardest on the new converts. They have only just begun to steep their ears in divine sermons; they are still infants, fresh from their old life, groping about with undeveloped vision. True, they renounce their past and take up repentance, yet they neglect to shut themselves inside it. For the very desire for something from that past cuts them off short—just as fruit that has already begun to wither or turn bitter still flatters itself with a trace of its former sweetness. Moreover, every fault of hesitation and evasion toward repentance carries the presumption of baptism. Certain of unquestioned forgiveness, they steal the interim and issue themselves a license to sin, not instruction to avoid it. How foolish, how unjust: to skip repentance yet claim forgiveness—that is, to refuse the price and still reach for the merchandise. The Lord established that price for granting pardon; with this repentance-payment he offers to redeem impunity. If merchants test the coin before they strike a bargain, lest it be counterfeit, clipped, or adulterated, do we really believe the Lord submits repentance to prior testing before granting so great a reward as eternal life? But let us put off the truth of repentance for a moment. Do you suppose the corrected will be obvious once we are absolved? Not at all. While pardon still hangs in the balance, punishment looms; we do not yet merit release so that we may merit it when God threatens, not when he forgives. What servant, once freed, charges himself with his own thefts and escapes? What soldier, once discharged, still answers for his old offenses? The sinner must lament before forgiveness, because the time for repentance is a time of danger and fear. I do not deny that the divine benefit—the abolition of sins—is entirely secure for those initiated into the water; but reaching it demands effort. Who would grant even a single sprinkling of any water to a man of such faithless repentance? Stealthy assault and self-serving assertions come easily. But God guards his treasure and does not let the unworthy sneak in. What does he finally say? Nothing hidden will stay unrevealed. However much darkness you pile over your deeds, God is light. Some, however, imagine God is obliged to deliver his promise even to the unworthy, turning his liberality into a form of servitude. If he grants the sign of death out of necessity, he does it unwillingly; and who lets stand what he gave unwillingly? Do not many fall away afterward? Is that gift not taken from many? These are the infiltrators who, having assaulted the pledge of repentance, build a house doomed to collapse on sand. So let no one flatter himself just because he is counted among the novices, as if he may still sin now that he has come to know the Lord; let him fear and revere at the same time. But what does it profit you to have known, when you lie in the very things you were ignorant of before? What separates you from a perfect servant of God? Is Christ one thing to the baptized and another to the hearers? Is there another hope, another reward, another fear of judgment, another necessity of repentance? That washing is the seal of a faith which begins with and is commended by the faith of repentance. We are not washed so that we may cease to sin, since we have already been washed in heart. For this is the hearer’s first washing: a whole fear; from then on, as long as you sense the Lord, you possess sound faith, a conscience that has once embraced repentance. Yet if we stop sinning after the waters, we put on innocence by compulsion, not free will. Who then excels in goodness? To whom is evil not permitted, or displeasing? Who is commanded, and who delights, to be free of crime? So we do not turn our hands from theft unless prison’s harshness stops us; we do not restrain our eyes from lust unless bodyguards block us. If no one devoted to the Lord stops sinning unless bound by baptism, I cannot tell whether such a baptized man grieves more over having stopped sinning than he rejoices over having escaped. Therefore hearers ought to desire baptism, not presume it. He who desires honors; he who presumes is proud. In the one appears modesty; in the other, petulance. The one strives; the other neglects. The one wants to merit; the other promises himself the debt: the one receives; the other invades. Whom do you judge more worthy, if not the more corrected? Whom more corrected, if not the more fearful, and therefore the one who has performed true repentance? He still feared to sin, lest he fail to merit receiving. But the presumptuous man, secure in his self-made promise, could not fear; thus he did not fulfill repentance, because he lacked its instrument—fear. Presumption is a slice of shamelessness; it crowds the petitioner and despises the giver. Consequently it sometimes deceives. For it promises before the debt is due, and the one who must pay is always offended.
